items.text: Carbonates are not mentioned as bases on the syllabus; only metal oxides, metal hydroxides and ammonia.

items.label: text
items.text: All neutralisation reactions for an acid reacting with an alkali have the same ionic equation: they all involve the hydroxide ions from the alkali reacting with the H⁺ ions from the acid to form water.

items.label: text
items.text: Carbonates react with cold dilute acids to produce carbon dioxide gas.

items.label: text
items.text: A summary equation for acids and carbonates:

items.label: text
items.text: carbonate + acid → salt + carbon dioxide + water

items.label: text
items.text: Green copper(Ill) carbonate reacts with the common dilute acids to give a blue or blue-green solution of copper(ll) sulfate, copper(ll) nitrate or copper(Il) chloride. Carbon dioxide gas is given off. You can recognise this because it turns limewater milky.

items.label: text
items.text: All the equations have the same form:

items.label: text
items.text: CuCO3(s) + H2SO4(aq) → CuSO4(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O(l)

items.label: text
items.text: CuCO3(s) + 2HNO3(aq) → Cu(NO3)2(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O(l)

items.label: text
items.text: CuCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CuCl2(aq)+ CO2(g) + H_2O(I)
